questions_json.explanation: The independent variable is what the researcher changes — here, the music condition. The test scores are the dependent variable, the outcome being measured.
options: The test scores
Whether students listen to music or study in silence
The students' intelligence
The room temperature
questions_json.q: A researcher wants to know if listening to music helps students study. She divides students into two groups — one studies in silence, the other with music playing — then compares their test scores. What is the independent variable in this study?

questions_json.explanation: Random assignment spreads patient differences equally between groups, so any difference in results can be credited to the therapy, not to pre-existing differences between patients.
options: To make the therapy cheaper
To keep patients from talking to each other
To make the two groups equal on average so the comparison is fair
Because the law requires coin flips
questions_json.q: Dr. Ahmed is testing a new therapy for anxiety. He assigns patients to either the new therapy or the old therapy, deciding by flipping a coin for each patient. Why does he do this?

questions_json.explanation: A confound is an extra variable mixed up with the independent variable. Since the drink group also studied longer, the study's internal validity is broken — we cannot tell what really caused the higher scores.
options: The extra study time is a confounding variable — we cannot tell if the drink or the extra studying caused the improvement
Energy drinks are too expensive for a real study
The sample was too large to trust
The researchers should have used a survey instead
questions_json.q: A study claims a new energy drink improves exam scores. But the group that drank it also studied longer than the group that did not. What is the problem with this study's conclusion?

questions_json.explanation: Reliability means consistency. A reliable measure gives similar results under similar conditions (test-retest reliability). This questionnaire fails that test.
options: The patient is lying
The questionnaire is too long
The questionnaire lacks validity
The questionnaire lacks reliability — it should give consistent results when nothing has changed
questions_json.q: A clinic gives the same depression questionnaire to a patient on Monday and again on Friday. The patient's life has not changed, but the two scores are wildly different. What is the problem?

questions_json.explanation: Correlation only shows two things moving together. A third variable (summer heat) can explain both — this is why 'correlation does not imply causation' is a core rule of research.
options: Eating ice cream causes drowning
The two are correlated, but a third factor (hot weather) likely explains both — correlation does not prove causation
Drowning makes people buy more ice cream
The data must be wrong
questions_json.q: Researchers find that ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together in the summer months. What is the correct conclusion?

questions_json.explanation: A p-value below 0.05 means the result would rarely happen by chance alone. It does not mean the effect is large or certain — only that it is unlikely to be a fluke.
options: The drug works 95% of the time
95% of patients were cured
The result is definitely due to chance
There is less than a 5% chance the result is due to random luck alone, so researchers treat it as statistically significant
questions_json.q: A study reports that a memory drug improved scores with 'p < 0.05'. What does this mean?

questions_json.explanation: A convenience sample (whoever is easy to reach) may not represent the whole population. Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance and produces more trustworthy results.
options: Her class is too intelligent to count
She should have asked teachers instead
Her sample is not representative — one class cannot stand in for all students in the country
Surveys never produce useful data
questions_json.q: A researcher wants to know what all university students in the country think about online exams. She only asks students from her own class. What is the sampling problem?

questions_json.explanation: Informed consent is a core ethics rule: people must understand what they are signing up for and agree freely. Debriefing (fully explaining the study) happens after the study, not before.
options: Informed consent — participants must understand the study and agree freely before it begins
Debriefing
Random assignment
Peer review
questions_json.q: Before joining a psychology experiment, participants are told what the study involves, that they can leave at any time, and they sign a form agreeing to take part. What is this called?

questions_json.explanation: A placebo control plus blinding rules out the placebo effect. Any extra improvement in the real-pill group can then be credited to the pill itself rather than to expectation.
options: To save money on pills
To punish the control group
Because sugar pills are healthier
The sugar pill group is a control — it shows whether improvement comes from the pill itself or just from expecting to improve
questions_json.q: A company tests a new 'focus pill'. One group gets the real pill, another gets an identical-looking sugar pill, and neither group knows which they received. Why include the sugar pill group?

questions_json.explanation: Reliability is consistency (this test is consistent); validity is whether it measures what it claims to measure (this test misses its target). A test can be reliable without being valid.
options: The test is valid but not reliable
The test is neither reliable nor valid
The test is reliable but not valid — it measures consistently, but not the right thing
The test is both reliable and valid
questions_json.q: A test always gives the same score when repeated, but it was designed to measure anxiety and actually measures general stress instead. Which statement is true?
